quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the daily ledger, the ramp-up of looms, cumulative stock and container sizes.

questions.q: What does the Planning IV workbook simulate day by day?
options: Looms coming on line, production, cumulative stock and shipments
questions.explain: The daily ledger multiplies looms running by the rate per loom, adds to stock, and subtracts shipments on their dates to see whether each shipment is covered.

questions.q: The 68" quality of 60×60/161×112 makes how many metres per loom per day in the lecture?
questions.explain: The lecture gives 230 m per loom per day for the 68" quality and 170 m for the wider 98" quality.

questions.q: 'Ramp-up' in this lecture means:
options: Releasing looms to the order gradually, one more every few days, until all are running
questions.explain: Looms are added one every two days for the 68" and every two and a half days for the 98", so production climbs in steps rather than starting at full rate.

questions.q: In the lecture's simulation day 1 corresponds to 1 September and 10 October is day 40.
questions.explain: September has 30 days, so 10 October is day 40; 25 October is 55, 5 November is 66 and 30 November is 91.

questions.q: A 20 ft container holds how much of the 98" quality?
questions.explain: The lecture states 40,000 m of 68" or 30,000 m of 98" per 20 ft box; the wider fabric takes more space per metre, so fewer metres fit.

questions.q: A 40 ft container holds, compared with a 20 ft box:
questions.explain: A 40 ft box holds double: 80,000 m of 68" or 60,000 m of 98", or a mix such as 40,000 m of 68" plus 30,000 m of 98".

questions.q: 'Cumulative stock' on a given day means:
options: All production to date minus all shipments made to date
The stock in the yarn store
questions.explain: The ledger carries stock forward: each day adds production and subtracts any shipment loaded, so the running total is what is physically in the warehouse.

questions.q: A negative result on a shipment day in the worksheet means the stock exceeded the shipment.
questions.explain: The sheet reports stock after loading; a negative figure means the stock fell short of the shipment — the shipment slips.

questions.q: Why does the lecture single out the 98" quality as 'the one to watch'?
options: Its margin after the first two shipments is thinner, about 18,500 m
questions.explain: After the first two shipments the 98" stock in hand is only about 18,500 m, so a slower release of its looms would make a shipment slip first.

questions.q: The 'day on which the last shipment is fully covered' (57 for 68", 71 for 98") tells the planner:
options: When the last loom was released
The day cumulative production first equals the total of all four shipments
When the last container is loaded
The day the order was booked
questions.explain: It is the day on which production to date reaches the total of all shipments — well before the last shipment date of day 91 in both cases.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How looms, rates, ramp intervals and shipment dates combine in the daily ledger, and which way the result moves.

questions.q: Daily production of a quality in the ledger is:
options: Looms running that day × metres per loom per day
Maximum looms × metres per loom per day
questions.explain: Only the looms actually released by that day produce; during the ramp the count is below the maximum, which is why early stock builds slowly.

questions.q: With one loom on day 1 and one more every two days, the looms running on day d (before the maximum is reached) are:
options: 1 + the whole number of completed 2-day intervals since day 1
questions.explain: Day 1 and 2 have 1 loom, days 3 and 4 have 2, and so on: 1 + floor((d − 1) ÷ 2). Simply d ÷ 2 gives half a loom on day 1.

questions.q: Shortening the release interval from one loom every 2.5 days to one every 2 days will:
options: Reduce the stock on every shipment day
Raise the stock on every shipment day by bringing production forward
Have no effect once all looms are running
questions.explain: Faster release means more loom-days early on; the extra production carries forward in stock to every later date, even after the loom count has levelled off.

questions.q: Once all looms are running, cumulative stock between shipments grows by a constant amount each day.
questions.explain: With the maximum looms the daily production is fixed (e.g. 12 × 230 = 2,760 m for the 68"), so the stock line is straight between shipment steps.

questions.q: Stock on a shipment day after loading equals:
options: Cumulative production to that day − cumulative shipments including that day
Production that day − shipment that day
questions.explain: The ledger subtracts every shipment made up to and including the date; a positive remainder is the margin, a negative one a shortfall.

questions.q: Moving a shipment date earlier, with the same quantity, will:
options: Increase the stock available on that date
Reduce the stock available on that date and may make it slip
questions.explain: Fewer days of production have accumulated by an earlier date, so the margin shrinks; the simulation shows at once whether it turns negative.

questions.q: The number of 20 ft-container-equivalents a shipment occupies is found by:
questions.explain: Each quality has its own capacity per box, so each is divided by its own figure and the fractions added. Pooling the metres ignores that 98" takes more room.

questions.q: If the metres per loom per day of the 98" quality fall from 170 to 150 because of lower efficiency, the first shipment margin of 18,450 m will:
questions.explain: Production to day 40 is 285 loom-days × rate; at 150 m that is 42,750 m instead of 48,450 m, so stock after the 30,000 m shipment drops to 12,750 m.

questions.q: The maximum number of looms on a quality does not affect the stock on any shipment day once the ramp is complete.
questions.explain: The maximum fixes the daily rate after the ramp; more looms mean more metres every day, so every later shipment margin rises.

questions.q: Total production over a period = Σ(looms on each day) × rate. The sum of looms over the days is called:
questions.explain: Loom-days count one loom running one day; multiplied by the metres per loom per day they give the output for the period.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Ledger arithmetic with the lecture's rates, ramps and shipments, and the containers they fill.

questions.q: The 68" quality starts with 1 loom on day 1 and gains one loom every 2 days up to 12 looms. By day 40 it has accumulated 348 loom-days. At 230 m per loom-day, what is the cumulative production on day 40?
questions.explain: 348 × 230 = 80,040 m produced by 10 October.

questions.q: Cumulative 68" production on day 40 is 80,040 m and the 10 October shipment is 40,000 m. What is the stock after loading?
questions.explain: 80,040 − 40,000 = 40,040 m remain in stock, matching the worksheet.

questions.q: From day 41 to day 55 the 68" quality runs its full 12 looms at 230 m each. How many metres are produced in those 15 days?
68" stock after the day-40 shipment is 40,040 m; 41,400 m are produced by day 55, when 45,000 m are shipped. What is the stock after loading on day 55?
questions.explain: 40,040 + 41,400 − 45,000 = 36,440 m, as the worksheet shows for the 25 October shipment.

questions.q: The 98" quality accumulates 285 loom-days by day 40 at 170 m per loom-day and then ships 30,000 m. What is the stock after loading?
The 98" quality has 18,950 m in stock after day 55 and runs 10 looms at 170 m. On day 66 it ships 15,000 m. Stock after loading on day 66?

The four 98" shipments total 100,000 m. After day 66 the stock is 22,650 m with 70,000 m already shipped, and 10 looms add 1,700 m a day. On which day number is the full 100,000 m first covered? (Round up to a whole day.)
questions.explain: Still needed: 100,000 − 70,000 − 22,650 = 7,350 m; ÷ 1,700 = 4.3 days, so day 66 + 5 = day 71 (day 70 reaches only 6,800 m).

questions.q: The 5 November lot is 20,000 m of 68" and 15,000 m of 98". Expressed as 20 ft-container equivalents (40,000 m of 68" or 30,000 m of 98" per box), how much space does it need? Answer to two decimals.
questions.explain: 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.00 — the lot exactly fills one 20 ft container, as the lecture notes.

questions.q: A shipment of 40,000 m of 68" plus 30,000 m of 98" needs:
questions.explain: 40,000 ÷ 40,000 + 30,000 ÷ 30,000 = 2 twenty-foot equivalents, which is one 40 ft box. A single 20 ft box takes only half of it.

questions.q: With 12 looms at 230 m, how many days of full production does the 45,000 m 25 October shipment represent?
questions.explain: 45,000 ÷ 2,760 = 16.3 days of full output. 20 days would be the figure at 2,250 m a day, and 27 days ignores seven of the looms.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Using the ramp-up simulation to answer the questions a planner and a merchandiser actually ask.

questions.q: The customer asks to pull the 25 October shipment of 98" forward to 15 October. The quickest way to answer is to:
options: Change the shipment day in the worksheet from 55 to 45 and read the result cell
questions.explain: The sheet re-runs the ledger instantly; the result for that shipment shows whether the stock is still positive after loading.

questions.q: The 98" looms are being released every 3 days instead of every 2.5 because of a sizing bottleneck. The planner should expect:
options: No change — the maximum looms is the same
Lower stock on every shipment day, with the thin 98" margins at risk first
Higher stock, because the looms rest
Only the last shipment to be affected
questions.explain: A slower ramp loses loom-days early, and the loss carries forward to every later date; the lecture flags the 98" quality precisely because its margin is thin.

questions.q: The 68" stock after loading on day 91 is 95,800 m, far more than needed. The merchandiser could:
options: Offer the customer an extra or earlier shipment, or release some 68" looms to other orders sooner
Slow the looms to waste less
questions.explain: Surplus stock is tied-up capital; the simulation shows capacity could be freed or an additional shipment booked. Cloth of one width cannot be sold as another.

questions.q: If a shipment is short by 2,000 m on its date, splitting that 2,000 m into the next shipment is one practical remedy to discuss with the customer.
questions.explain: A small shortfall can often be deferred to the following container with the customer's agreement; the ledger shows whether the next date can absorb it.

questions.q: Which change would most quickly repair a 98" shortfall on the 10 October shipment?
options: Adding a 98" loom from day 1 rather than waiting for the ramp
questions.explain: Only loom-days before day 40 help the first shipment; a loom from day 1 adds 40 × 170 = 6,800 m by then. A loom on day 60 or a 68" change is irrelevant to that date.

questions.q: Shipping department asks whether the 10 October lot (40,000 m of 68" and 30,000 m of 98") can go in two 20 ft boxes instead of one 40 ft. The answer is:
options: Yes — one box of each quality, each exactly full
No — a 20 ft box holds only 20,000 m
Yes, but three boxes are needed
questions.explain: 40,000 m of 68" fills one 20 ft box and 30,000 m of 98" fills another, so two 20 ft boxes carry the same as one 40 ft; the choice is a freight-rate question.

questions.q: The simulation shows every shipment covered, but the loom plan from Lecture 19 assumed 96 % A-grade. If the ledger used gross production, the risk is:
options: Stock in the ledger is overstated by the B-grade share, so thin margins could really be shortfalls
No risk — grading happens after shipping
questions.explain: Only A-grade cloth can be shipped; 4 % of 48,450 m is nearly 2,000 m, enough to matter where the margin is thin. The ledger's rate should be net of grading.

questions.q: A daily ledger is unnecessary when all looms start on day 1 at full rate, because stock then grows at a constant rate and a single multiplication gives it on any date.
questions.explain: The ledger earns its keep during the ramp and around shipments; with constant production the stock on any day is simply rate × days minus shipments to date.

questions.q: Two shipments fall on consecutive days. The planner wants to know whether the second is safe. The ledger must:
options: Subtract the first shipment before checking the second
questions.explain: Stock is cumulative: the first loading reduces what is available for the second. Checking each shipment against gross production would overstate the second's cover.

questions.q: A new booking wants 25,000 m of 68" on 20 November (day 81). Using the worksheet, the planner should check:
options: The 68" stock after loading on day 81 with the extra shipment entered, and that the later 30 November shipment stays positive
questions.explain: An inserted shipment reduces stock for every later date, so both the new date and the following shipment must stay non-negative in the simulation.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder ledger reasoning: loom-day sums, ramps and margins, and the mistakes that make a safe shipment look short.

questions.q: The 68" ramp adds one loom every 2 days from 1 loom on day 1, up to a maximum of 12. Looms 1–12 are therefore all running from day 23. How many loom-days accumulate by day 40? (Hint: 2 × (1 + 2 + … + 11) for days 1–22, then 12 looms for days 23–40.)
questions.explain: Days 1–22 give 2 × 66 = 132 loom-days; days 23–40 give 18 × 12 = 216; total 348 loom-days.

questions.q: If the 68" looms were all 12 from day 1 instead of ramping, how many extra metres would be in stock on day 40 compared with the ramped 348 loom-days? Rate 230 m per loom-day.
questions.explain: 480 − 348 = 132 loom-days lost to the ramp; × 230 = 30,360 m — the cost of releasing looms gradually.

questions.q: A student sums the 98" ramp as 1 + 2 + 3 + … up to day 40 and gets far more than 285 loom-days. The error is:
options: Forgetting that each loom count persists for 2.5 days and that the count stops at the maximum of 10
questions.explain: Looms are added one every 2.5 days, not every day, and never exceed 10; the loom count on each day must be summed, not the loom numbers.

questions.q: The 98" quality has 10 looms at 170 m. Stock after the day-66 shipment is 22,650 m. The 30 November (day 91) shipment is 30,000 m. What is the stock after loading on day 91?

Suppose the 98" shipments were instead 30,000 m on day 40 and 40,000 m on day 55, with 10 looms at 170 m from day 41 and 18,450 m in stock after day 40. What would the stock be after loading on day 55? (A negative answer means short.)
questions.explain: 15 × 1,700 = 25,500 m; 18,450 + 25,500 − 40,000 = 3,950 m — covered, but with almost no margin.

questions.q: The last 68" shipment is fully covered on day 57 although it ships on day 91. This means:
options: All 125,000 m of the four shipments have been produced by day 57, so 68" looms could be released after that
The shipment must be moved to day 57
The stock is negative on day 57
The 68" looms must run to day 91
questions.explain: By day 57 cumulative production exceeds the total booked, so later production only builds surplus; those looms are capacity for new orders.

questions.q: Total 68" shipments are 125,000 m and 12 looms give 2,760 m a day. After day 55 the cumulative production is 121,440 m. How many whole days after day 55 are needed to cover the full 125,000 m?
questions.explain: Short by 3,560 m; 3,560 ÷ 2,760 = 1.29, so 2 whole days — day 57, as the worksheet reports.

questions.q: The ledger counts day 1 as 1 September and uses 40 for 10 October. A student who starts counting at day 0 on 1 September will:
options: Give every shipment one more day of production than it really has
Give every shipment one less day of production
questions.explain: Shifting the calendar by one day adds a day's output before each shipment date and makes a borderline shipment look safe when it is not.

questions.q: If a 20 ft container is booked for the 25 October lot of 45,000 m of 68" plus 25,000 m of 98", it will be over-full.
questions.explain: 45,000 ÷ 40,000 + 25,000 ÷ 30,000 = 1.125 + 0.833 = 1.96 twenty-foot equivalents, so it needs a 40 ft box (capacity 2.0), not a 20 ft one.

questions.q: Which of these would NOT change the day on which the last 98" shipment is fully covered?
options: Raising the rate from 170 to 180 m
Releasing looms every 2 days instead of 2.5
Moving the 5 November shipment to 10 November without changing its quantity
questions.explain: The coverage day depends on cumulative production reaching the total shipped, not on when individual shipments fall; rate, ramp and loom count all change production.
